part_title: RAG Observability, AI Incident Response and Production Readiness

scenes.title: RAG Observability Pipeline
scenes.narration: Follow this RAG pipeline from ingestion through chunking, embedding, vector search and answer generation. Each stage transforms the information and also creates a different class of monitoring problem. During ingestion, the system must track whether source documents are current and whether incremental updates have completed. Chunking should preserve enough context and metadata, and the embedding stage needs consistent model and version information. Vector search must retrieve relevant passages, while the generator should cite them and abstain when evidence is unavailable. The lower dashboard measures these responsibilities separately. Document freshness tells us whether sources remain current. Retrieval hit rate checks whether top K contains relevant evidence. Citation coverage checks how often answers include sources, and groundedness measures whether factual claims are supported. No-answer rate helps detect failures to abstain when a question lacks evidence. The sample percentages are illustrative, not universal service objectives. If an answer becomes stale, don't automatically switch the foundation model. First ask whether source updates reached the index, whether retrieval filters excluded the correct document, and whether the final response used the returned context. This is why RAG observability must cover the whole pipeline.

scenes.title: AI Incident Response Workflow
scenes.narration: This slide is a response playbook for when an AI application begins misbehaving. Follow the steps left to right. An alarm or user complaint detects an issue. The team triages the impact, scope and severity, then examines traces and logs to locate the failing operation. In the example, the dashboard shows elevated errors and long latency, while a trace reveals a retrieval dependency timing out. Next, classify the problem. A model issue might produce unsafe or unexpected content. A retrieval issue might return missing or outdated passages. A dependency incident could involve a failed database or tool, while a security issue might involve prompt injection or a data leak. Mitigation should match the category: roll back an unsafe prompt, correct an index, fail over to a validated dependency or restrict traffic. Finally, record the incident, evidence, actions and preventive changes. Notice that alerting and remediation are not the same thing. Every action must be reversible where practical and guided by impact and safety, not merely by the first suspicious metric. A post-incident review adds new evaluation cases and monitoring so the same problem is easier to catch next time.

scenes.title: Production readiness checklist for a GenAI release
scenes.narration: This slide is a pre-production checklist, and every column represents a release obligation. Begin with an evaluation baseline: has the candidate met its predefined quality and business objectives? Continue to safety testing against harmful content, prompt injection and policy failures. The next columns require working dashboards, routed alarms and useful traces so operators can detect and diagnose trouble after deployment. The lower row covers safe rollback, cost budgets, data privacy, access control and an operational runbook. These aren't independent nice-to-have features. For example, a release with strong offline evaluation but no rollback path can still become a serious production problem. The decision panel on the right has only two outcomes: promote when all critical requirements are met, or hold when something important remains open. Promotion should start with a small traffic percentage and expand only after the relevant metrics remain healthy. One privacy caveat: the slide mentions traces with inputs and outputs, but sensitive raw model content should only be captured under an explicitly approved logging policy. Useful telemetry normally relies on redacted fields and identifiers. A production-ready AI feature is one the team can evaluate, observe, secure and recover.

scenes.title: X-Ray Advantages for AI Applications
scenes.narration: Look at the complete AI request across the top. API Gateway receives the question, an orchestrator calls retrieval, a prompt builder prepares context, model invocation generates content, and a formatter returns the answer. A vector database, model endpoint and cache appear as downstream dependencies. Now examine the four benefits in the lower half. First, X-Ray can expose performance bottlenecks by showing which component consumes the most time. Second, it discovers service dependencies, allowing operators to see which backends are affected when one service slows down. Third, it helps investigate exceptions and error patterns, including a model service returning a throttling response. Fourth, it connects a particular request's timeline and status across instrumented services. The slide's sample trace shows relatively short API work and a longer model invocation. Treat those figures as examples, not performance requirements. X-Ray isn't a foundation-model evaluator; it tells you how requests moved and where time or failures accumulated. To judge whether an answer was correct or grounded, pair traces with RAG evaluation and application metrics. The strongest troubleshooting combines service evidence with output-quality evidence.

scenes.title: Trace a Synchronous AI Request End to End
scenes.narration: This diagram follows a single synchronous question-answer request. The user sends a question through API Gateway, which attaches or propagates the tracing context and invokes Lambda. Lambda validates the request and queries the retrieval store for relevant chunks. Those chunks return to Lambda, which builds a prompt and invokes Amazon Bedrock. The model response is then formatted and returned to the client. The lower timeline uses one trace identifier to connect all these interactions and labels the request's total duration at about one point three eight seconds. Why is the distinction between spans and requests important? A retrieval subsegment can reveal database latency without losing the relationship to the overall user response. But when spans are nested, don't add every displayed duration as though they occurred independently. Track the actual critical path. Synchronous requests also have a user-visible waiting time and API timeout constraints. If model generation cannot finish within the allowed window, use an asynchronous job pattern rather than simply increasing retries. The purpose of this slide is to teach what one complete trace shows, from the original HTTP request to the final answer.
